intro.html: Who is in charge, and how? These words name kinds of power. Many of them are built from Greek parts: -archy and -cracy both mean rule, and the first part tells you who rules or how. auto- means self, olig- means few, and an- means without.
autocrat = self + power (one person rules alone). oligarchy = few + rule. anarchy = without + rule. bureaucracy = desk + rule (rule by offices and forms). hierarchy = a ranking from top to bottom.
These are words for history and the news, but the pictures here are fairy-tale kingdoms and clubhouses: the ideas are the same at any size.

words.def: having supreme power; independent and self-governing
words.ex: After a long struggle, the island became a {sovereign} nation with its own flag.
words.ctx: The treaty recognized the little kingdom as {sovereign}: no larger country could tax its people or overrule its laws.
words.etym: From Old French soverain, “highest, supreme,” from Latin super (above).
words.note: As a noun, a sovereign is a king or queen.

mn.text: The little island kingdom reigns over itself and takes orders from no one. It is {sovereign}.

scene.alt: A proud queen raises her scepter on her own small island, beside its flag.

words.def: the freedom to govern yourself or make your own choices
words.ex: At college, Maya enjoyed the {autonomy} of planning her own days.
words.ctx: The branch library was granted more {autonomy}; instead of waiting for orders from the main office, its staff could now choose their own books and hours.

mn.cue: AUTO = SELF: you set your own rules
mn.text: On her birthday, Maya gets her own key and her own schedule: she decides where to go and when. She has {autonomy}.

scene.alt: A teen happily holds up her own key while her mother waves.

words.def: a ruler who holds total power alone
words.ex: The old czar was an {autocrat} who answered to no parliament.
words.ctx: The club’s founder ran it like an {autocrat}, making every decision himself and never once asking the members to vote.
words.etym: From Greek autokrates, “ruling by oneself”: autos (self) + kratos (power).

mn.text: King Victor signs every order himself and waves away his advisers: “I decide!” A ruler who holds all the power alone is an {autocrat}.

scene.alt: A king signs every order himself and ignores his worried adviser.

words.def: a ruler who uses total power cruelly
words.ex: In the legend, a {despot} took half of every farmer’s harvest.
words.ctx: Unlike his fair-minded father, the young king became a {despot}, jailing anyone who complained and raising taxes whenever he liked.

mn.text: The cruel king marches into the village and takes every pot of soup for himself, leaving the people hungry. He is a {despot}.

scene.alt: A cruel king carries off the village soup pot while a grandmother and a boy look on sadly.

words.def: cruel and unjust use of power
words.ex: The rebels fought to free their land from {tyranny}.
words.ctx: Under the old baron’s {tyranny}, villagers could be fined for singing in the street, and no one dared to complain.
words.etym: From Greek tyrannos, “absolute ruler,” the same word that gave the dinosaur Tyrannosaurus its name.

mn.text: King Rex makes the townspeople bow every time he passes and punishes anyone who sneezes. His cruel, unjust rule is {tyranny}.

scene.alt: A cruel king in a crown orders frightened townspeople to bow.

words.def: dominance of one group or nation over others
words.ex: For centuries the city held {hegemony} over trade on the river.
words.ctx: The kingdom never conquered its small neighbors, but its {hegemony} was clear: its coins, its laws and its fleet set the terms that everyone else had to follow.

mn.text: One giant hedge spreads over the whole street until every garden sits in its shade. That hedge’s {hegemony} is complete.

scene.alt: A giant hedge towers over the little gardens of a street while a neighbor stares in surprise.

words.def: a system run by many officials and complicated rules
words.ex: Getting a permit meant months of {bureaucracy} and forms.
words.ctx: The new mayor promised to cut through the {bureaucracy}; instead of six offices and ten forms, a building permit would need one visit and one page.

mn.cue: BUREAU-CRACY: rule by desks and forms
mn.text: To get a library card, Pip fills out Form A, gets a stamp at Desk B, waits in Line C and is sent back to Form A. That maze of offices is {bureaucracy}.

scene.alt: A bored clerk at a desk sends a confused boy holding a pile of forms to the next window.

words.def: a system that ranks people or things one above another
words.ex: In the army’s {hierarchy}, a general outranks a colonel, and a colonel outranks a captain.
words.ctx: The kitchen ran on a strict {hierarchy}: the head chef gave orders to the cooks, the cooks to the helpers, and the helpers to the new dishwasher.
words.etym: From Greek hierarkhia, “rule of a high priest”: hieros (sacred) + arkhein (to rule); later, any ranking from top to bottom.

mn.text: At the castle the king stands highest, then the knight, then the cook. That ranking from higher to lower is a {hierarchy}.

scene.alt: A cook, a knight and a king stand on stacks of crates, each one higher than the last.

words.def: rule by a small group of people
words.ex: The city was run by an {oligarchy} of five wealthy merchant families.
words.ctx: Although the club claimed to be open to all, it was really an {oligarchy}: three senior members made every decision and never put anything to a vote.
words.etym: From Greek oligarkhia: oligos (few) + arkhein (to rule).
words.note: Oligarchy is rule by a few; monarchy is rule by one.

mn.text: Ollie and his two best friends make every rule for the whole treehouse club; the other kids get no say. Rule by a few like that is an {oligarchy}.

labels.text: OLIG = FEW: rule by a FEW

scene.alt: Three boys in paper crowns stand on a bench making the rules while a girl crosses her arms.

words.def: a lack of government or control; disorder
words.ex: When the referee left, the game dissolved into {anarchy}.
words.ctx: With no captain and no rules, the ship’s crew fell into {anarchy}: everyone gave orders, no one followed them, and the sails flapped loose for days.
words.etym: From Greek anarkhia, “lack of a leader”: an (without) + arkhos (ruler).
words.note: Strictly, anarchy means no ruler; in everyday use it means chaos.

mn.text: The teacher steps out for five minutes, and with no one in charge the room turns to chaos: paper planes, spilled paint, kids on desks. That is {anarchy}.

scene.alt: With no teacher in the room, children dance on desks and throw papers in a wild mess.

who rules
parts
after.cap: The parts tell you who holds the power.

after.html: Sovereign and autonomy are about freedom from outside control: a sovereign nation answers to no other nation, and a person with autonomy makes her own choices. Hegemony is the opposite situation seen from above: one power dominating the rest.

items.q: A country ruled by a handful of rich families is an…
items.why: Olig- means few: oligarchy is rule by a small group. Monarchy (one) and anarchy (none) are different.

items.q: True or false: the Greek parts of anarchy mean “without a ruler.”
items.why: True. An- means without and -archy means rule. In everyday use anarchy has come to mean chaos.

items.q: Which word has a part that means “self”?
items.why: Auto- means self: an autocrat rules by himself, with no one to answer to.

items.q: Type the word for a system of many officials, offices and forms (it begins with the French word for desk).
